An audience is not a business

Strategy · Media

In short: an audience is an asset, not a business. A media business starts when you can say who the audience is, what it does, who pays for access to it, and which part of it you actually own.

Key points

  • A media company sells to readers, sponsors and licensees, plus investors, and each buys something different.
  • Reach is the weakest claim; state what the audience does: decides, buys or builds.
  • Report the owned audience first and separately; rented platform reach exists to feed the owned list.
  • In media the product truth is the editorial point of view, written as one sentence someone could disagree with.
  • Tag every external audience number as verified, platform-reported or estimated, and keep estimates out of the deck without a method.

Three buyers and an investor

Most media founders pitch one thing to everyone: size. That fails because a media company sells to at least three different buyers, and each one is buying something different.

Readers and subscribers buy time saved, judgement they trust, or access they cannot get elsewhere. Advertisers and sponsors buy attention from a specific kind of person at a specific moment. Licensees and data buyers buy content or signals they can use inside their own products. Then there is the investor, who buys the future cash flows of all of the above.

Part 2 covers one product truth and a belief per audience. In media, that discipline matters more, because the buyers are so unlike each other. The reader does not care about your CPM. The sponsor does not care about your editorial mission unless it explains who reads you.

Write the four beliefs down. If two of them are the same sentence, you have not done the work.

Reach is the weakest claim

Reach is easy to state and easy to discount. Everyone has a number, most of them are platform-reported, and buyers have learned to divide them by something.

The stronger claim is about composition and behaviour. Who are these people, and what do they do? Three verbs matter most to the people who pay you:

Verb What it means for the audience Who pays for it
Decides Signs off budgets, policy, hiring, vendors Sponsors, B2B data buyers
Buys Purchases in a category you cover Affiliates, commerce partners, sponsors
Builds Ships products or code in your field Tooling sponsors, recruiters, licensees

A small audience that decides outperforms a large audience that scrolls. Your positioning should state the verb, the category, and the proof.

"Read by people who run treasury at mid-sized funds" is a position. "Two hundred thousand followers" is a number.

Owned versus rented

Every media business has two audiences and only one of them is yours.

The owned audience is the list you can email, the members you can bill, the subscribers whose details sit in your systems. You set the rules, you can move platforms, and nobody can throttle you.

The rented audience is everyone who follows you on a platform. The platform owns the relationship, the algorithm, the data, and the right to change the terms tomorrow.

Rented reach has a job: it feeds the owned list. That is its whole purpose in a commercial model. If your rented numbers are growing and your owned numbers are flat, you are building someone else's asset.

Investors and serious sponsors already know this. State the owned number first, clearly and separately, and treat the rest as a funnel.

Editorial point of view is the product truth

In most verticals the product truth is a feature or an outcome. In media it is the point of view.

A point of view is what makes someone read you instead of the free summary. It is why a sponsor wants to appear next to you and not next to a competitor with the same audience size. It is why a licensee pays for your version of a story that exists elsewhere.

Write it in one sentence. It should be something a reasonable person in your field could disagree with. If nobody could disagree, it is not a point of view, it is a category description.

Everything downstream, from the subscription pitch to the sponsor deck, should be able to trace back to that sentence.

A claims register for audience numbers

Part 2 introduced the claims register. Media needs its own version because audience figures are the claims buyers check hardest.

Keep one sheet with every number you use externally. For each, record the source and the status:

  • Verified: from your own systems, exportable, auditable. Email list size, paid subscribers, renewal counts.
  • Platform-reported: from a dashboard you do not control. Followers, impressions, listens.
  • Estimated: derived or modelled. Household reach, pass-along, total audience.

Only verified numbers go in investor materials without a label. Platform-reported numbers get a label every time. Estimates stay out of the deck unless you can show the method.

This register is usually the first document we build with a media client, because it tends to change the pitch before anyone writes a slide.

The checklist

  • [ ] One belief written for each buyer: reader, sponsor, licensee, investor
  • [ ] Positioning states what the audience does, not how many there are
  • [ ] Owned audience reported separately from rented audience, owned first
  • [ ] Editorial point of view in one sentence someone could disagree with
  • [ ] Claims register with every external number tagged verified, platform-reported or estimated
  • [ ] Rented channels have an explicit job: feeding the owned list

Common questions

How should a media startup pitch its audience to investors and sponsors?

Write a separate belief for each buyer: reader, sponsor, licensee and investor. Position on what the audience does, such as deciding, buying or building, rather than how many people there are.

What is the difference between an owned and a rented audience?

The owned audience is the list you can email, the members you can bill and the subscribers in your own systems. The rented audience is your platform followers, where the platform owns the relationship, the algorithm and the data.

Which audience numbers can go in an investor deck?

Only verified numbers from your own systems go in without a label. Platform-reported numbers get a label every time, and estimates stay out unless you can show the method.

Is follower count a good way to sell a media business?

No. Reach is easy to state and easy to discount because most numbers are platform-reported. A small audience that decides outperforms a large audience that scrolls.
